I congratulate the Centre for Civil Society on the monumental publication of the Ease of
Operating School (EoOS) Index 2026. The hard work put in by the research team - Dr
Animesh, Shaivy and Nitesh deserves special attention for producing a study that combines
legal rigour with practical relevance. Incidentally, the privilege of personal experience is
confined to Dr Animesh only, but it is a sublime experience to bathe in the confidence of the
united efforts of the trio in this magnificent publication, which is pregnant with more future
useful publications.

The dedicated authors and the Centre for Civil Society appear to be inspired by the
admonition of the Gita “न िह $ानेन स(शं पिव-िमह िव/ते” (“There is nothing in this world as
purifying as knowledge”). The EoOS Index 2026 stands as a testament to an unwavering
dedication to the pursuit of knowledge, characterised by a steadfast adherence to scholarly
integrity and a profound concern for the collective good. Engaging in a thorough exploration
of the intricate and frequently disjointed regulatory structures that span various states is
indeed a formidable endeavour. The authors have deftly intertwined legal scholarship, policy
analysis, and empirical rigour to craft a work that addresses a significant void in the discourse
surrounding the governance of school education in India. The publication serves to deepen
our comprehension of the regulatory quandaries that educational institutions encounter,
whilst simultaneously establishing a robust groundwork for forthcoming inquiries, policy
transformations, and informed public discourse. I hold a firm belief that this groundbreaking
endeavour shall prove to be an invaluable asset for policymakers, scholars, educators, and the
myriad organisations that constitute civil society.

It is with profound sincerity that I extend my warmest regards to the esteemed authors and the
Centre for Civil Society, commending them on the fruition of this significant endeavour. May
this initiative herald a multitude of similar contributions in the unfolding years ahead.

                                                                      (Kamal Nayan Chaubey)

Competitive Federalism for Educational
Excellence
At the same time, the Index advances another
important constitutional value: competitive
federalism. Education is a Concurrent List subject,
and states possess substantial authority over
school regulation. Yet reform requires comparison.
What gets measured can be compared. What can
be compared can be improved. By evaluating
regulatory frameworks across states, the EoOS
Index creates a platform for mutual learning,
healthy competition, and evidence-based reform.

The findings suggest that schools operating
in different jurisdictions experience markedly

FINDING 5
Educational Performance and Regulatory
Accessibility Are Distinct Dimensions of
Governance
Several states traditionally associated with strong
educational outcomes perform below the national
average on the EoOS Index, while some states
facing broader educational governance challenges
emerge among the stronger performers.

The findings therefore suggest that educational
achievement and regulatory accessibility should
be treated as analytically distinct dimensions
of governance. Strong educational outcomes do
not necessarily imply an enabling regulatory
environment, just as regulatory accessibility does not
automatically translate into educational performance.

Conclusion

The findings of this chapter reveal a regulatory
architecture characterised not only by interstate
variation but also by an important structural
imbalance. Across states, regulatory systems
appear considerably more developed in areas
concerned with defining obligations, monitoring
compliance, and administering oversight than
in areas concerned with enabling sustainability,
adaptability, and autonomy. The challenge facing
policymakers is therefore not simply how much
regulation should exist, but how regulatory
systems can achieve a more effective balance
between accountability and enablement.

exercise of authority also requires safeguards that
promote fairness, predictability, and accountability.

The findings suggest that states differ substantially
in the extent to which such safeguards are
embedded within their regulatory frameworks.
Where procedural protections are limited, schools
may face greater uncertainty regarding inspections,
approvals, recognition decisions, and regulatory
enforcement. The challenge therefore lies not in
limiting authority but in ensuring that authority
operates within transparent and predictable
procedural frameworks.

A Regulatory System in Transition
Taken together, the findings suggest that
school regulation in India is best understood as
a system in transition. Across states, elements
of both traditional and emerging regulatory
approaches coexist. Some jurisdictions have
begun introducing more facilitative features
characterised by greater transparency, procedural
simplification, and institutional flexibility. Others
continue to rely primarily on compliance-oriented
approaches centred on approvals, oversight, and
administrative control. The resulting diversity
creates opportunities for comparative learning.

The next chapter develops a framework for
understanding these different approaches through
a set of regulatory archetypes derived from
observed patterns within the data.

The relevant question is not simply whether
a regulation has been published. The more
important question is whether a school can
reasonably find, understand, and comply with it.

Conclusion

The findings suggest that Regulatory Clarity,
Predictability and Accessibility constitutes one of
the strongest dimensions of school regulation in
India. Across states, regulations are increasingly
formalised, documented, and identifiable.
This reflects an important shift towards
more transparent and predictable systems of
governance. However, the domain also reveals that
visibility alone does not guarantee accessibility.
Schools continue to face challenges arising
from fragmented legal repositories, dispersed
administrative instruments, language barriers,
and procedural complexity.

The central lesson emerging from this domain
is straightforward. Schools cannot comply with
rules they cannot find or understand. Improving
regulatory quality therefore begins with making
regulation visible, accessible, and predictable.
Yet true ease of operation requires more than
clarity alone. It requires regulatory systems
that are not only understandable, but also
coherent, navigable, and ultimately supportive of
educational institutions.

Reform Priorities: Three broad reform priorities
emerge from the findings.

Rationalisation of Compliance Requirements:
States should periodically review existing
compliance obligations to identify duplicative,
outdated, or low-value requirements.

Risk-Based Regulation: Compliance intensity
should increasingly reflect institutional risk rather
than applying identical requirements to all schools
regardless of size, context, or compliance history.

Digital and Integrated Compliance Systems:
Where compliance requirements remain
necessary, they should be integrated through
simplified digital systems that minimise
duplication and administrative burden.

The objective should be to ensure that compliance
serves educational quality rather than becoming
an end in itself.

Conclusion

The findings reveal that compliance remains
the dominant organising principle of school
regulation across India. States have invested
considerable effort in constructing systems that
govern recognition, staffing, infrastructure,
financial reporting, and institutional
accountability. However, these systems often
impose substantial administrative obligations
upon schools.

The central lesson emerging from this domain
is that regulatory quality cannot be measured

Conclusion

The findings reveal that protection against
arbitrary regulatory action remains uneven
across India. Some states provide comparatively
stronger procedural safeguards, while others
continue to rely on regulatory frameworks where
discretionary authority is insufficiently structured.
The wide score range in this domain indicates
that schools in different states experience very
different levels of procedural certainty.

The central lesson is clear.Regulation becomes
legitimate when authority is accompanied by
accountability.

For schools, ease of operation depends not
only on clear rules and manageable compliance
obligations, but also on fair enforcement.
A regulatory system that is transparent but
discretionary remains incomplete. A truly enabling
framework must ensure that schools are not only
told what the rules are, but are also protected by
fair procedures when those rules are applied.

Conclusion

The findings reveal that Institutional Autonomy
remains one of the weaker dimensions of school
regulation in India. The challenge is not merely
administrative. It reflects a deeper question
regarding the relationship between educational
institutions and the State. Schools are expected
to deliver outcomes, manage resources, respond
to community needs, and continuously improve
educational quality. Yet many continue to operate
within frameworks that provide relatively limited
decision-making authority.

The central lesson emerging from this domain
is therefore straightforward. Educational
institutions cannot be fully effective if they
are denied meaningful agency. The strongest-
performing regulatory systems demonstrate that
accountability and autonomy are not opposing
principles. Rather, they are complementary
components of effective governance. The future
challenge for educational reform is not whether
schools should be regulated. It is whether
regulation can evolve from a framework centred
primarily on control towards one that combines
accountability, trust, institutional responsibility,
and educational excellence.

Ultimately, the quality of educational governance
depends not only on the standards imposed upon
schools, but also on the extent to which schools
are empowered to meet those standards.

The findings suggest that the next phase of
educational reform may require a shift in focus.
The first generation of reforms focused primarily
on expanding educational access. The second
generation focused increasingly on accountability,
standards, and compliance. The emerging
challenge is to build regulatory systems capable
of combining accountability with institutional
enablement. This requires moving beyond
the traditional debate between regulation and
deregulation. The question is not whether schools
should be regulated.

The question is whether regulation can be
designed in ways that strengthen educational
quality while simultaneously supporting
institutional sustainability, innovation,
adaptability, and autonomy. That is ultimately the
vision reflected in NEP 2020.

Conclusion

The findings of the Ease of Operating Schools
Index suggest that India’s regulatory architecture
is undergoing a gradual but incomplete transition.
States have made meaningful progress in
improving transparency, codification, procedural
visibility, and administrative modernisation.
These developments represent important steps
towards the governance philosophy articulated in
NEP 2020.

At the same time, substantial gaps remain.
Institutional autonomy remains constrained.
Financial sustainability remains weak. Lifecycle
flexibility remains limited. The separation-of-
functions agenda underpinning the SSSA reform
remains only partially realised across most states.
The challenge facing policymakers is therefore no
longer whether regulatory reform is necessary.
The challenge is how to complete the transition

Conclusion

The findings of the Ease of Operating Schools
Index reveal a regulatory architecture
characterised by an important structural
imbalance. Across states, regulatory systems
appear considerably more developed in
defining obligations, monitoring compliance,
and exercising oversight than in supporting
sustainability, adaptability, and institutional
autonomy. The result is a governance framework
marked by three interrelated deficits:
     • a Sustainability Deficit;
     • an Adaptability Deficit;
     • a Trust Deficit.

Taken together, these deficits help explain
many of the challenges identified throughout
the Index. The central lesson emerging from the
findings is therefore straightforward. The future
challenge for school regulation in India is not
simply improving compliance or strengthening
oversight. It is building a regulatory architecture
that combines accountability with enablement,
oversight with flexibility, and public interest with
institutional sustainability. Ultimately, schools
can only deliver educational outcomes if they are
not merely regulated, but also empowered
to succeed.

text:
Policy Pathway
Gujarat demonstrates relatively strong procedural safeguards against arbitrary regulatory action and
performs comparatively well in school lifecycle operations. However, these strengths are offset by weaker
performance in regulatory clarity, compliance requirements, financial flexibility, and institutional
autonomy. The state’s overall score of 17.90 out of 100 suggests that schools continue to face considerable
regulatory challenges despite the presence of certain procedural protections. Future reforms should
focus on improving regulatory predictability, simplifying compliance requirements, expanding financial
flexibility, and strengthening institutional autonomy. These changes would significantly improve the ease
of operating schools while preserving accountability and quality assurance mechanisms.

“   The mandate under Section 12 of the Act must be enforced
with conviction and commitment. We have to ensure admission
of at least twenty-five percent of class strength in unaided
schools with children of weaker and disadvantaged groups.
This is certainly a national mission. Effective implementation
of the statutory policy will be transformative and, in this
regard, each one of us, be it the institution or an individual, be
it the Central or the State Governments, Advisory Councils or
Commissions are duty bearers. The most important role is of the
neighbourhood schools. In this mission, the judiciary also bears
the burden to ensure that the process of admission is easily
accessible, effective and efficient. Court must also ensure that
judicial remedies against inaction or inefficiency are redressed
effectively and expeditiously.
                                                ”
                                              - Lucknow Public School v. State of U.P. 2026
                                                                       INSC 422 at para 12.

more predictable and enabling environment for schools.

Policy Pathway
Nagaland demonstrates that strong institutional autonomy can coexist with regulatory uncertainty. The
state ranks among the national leaders in institutional autonomy and performs well in school lifecycle
operations, allowing schools considerable flexibility in managing internal affairs and maintaining
operational continuity. However, its overall score of 20.04 out of 100 reflects significant constraints
arising from weak procedural safeguards, limited financial flexibility, and comparatively low regulatory
transparency. Given that more than two-thirds of students in Nagaland attend private schools, future
reforms should focus on improving transparency, strengthening protections against arbitrary regulatory
action, and expanding financial flexibility. These reforms would complement the state’s existing strengths
and create a more predictable and enabling environment for school operators.

text:
Policy Pathway
Odisha provides schools with a relatively stable and predictable regulatory environment, combining
above-average institutional autonomy with moderate levels of regulatory clarity, compliance ease, and
protection against arbitrary regulatory action. However, its overall score of 21.15 out of 100 highlights
continuing constraints on school sustainability and growth. The state’s weakest performance lies in
financial mobilization, where schools have limited flexibility to manage resources and plan for long-term
development. Additionally, procedural barriers associated with recognition, expansion, and institutional
restructuring continue to affect operational agility. Future reforms should focus on strengthening financial
autonomy and simplifying lifecycle-related processes while preserving the state’s existing strengths in
regulatory stability and procedural fairness.

“   It is one thing to say that the State may regulate the
fee structure of private unaided schools to ensure that the
school management does not indulge in profiteering and
commercialisation, but in the guise of exercise of that power,
it cannot transcend the line of regulation and impinge upon
the autonomy of the school to fix and collect “just” and
“permissible” school fees from its students. It is certainly not
an essential commodity governed by the legislation such as the
Essential Commodities Act, 1955 empowering the State to fix
tariff or price thereof.
                                    ”                     - Indian School v. State of Rajasthan,
                                                                  (2021) 10 SCC 517 at para 118.

Policy Pathway
Punjab combines strong school lifecycle processes, relatively predictable compliance systems, and
safeguards against arbitrary regulatory intervention, making it one of the more conducive regulatory
environments for private schools in India. The state’s top national ranking in School Lifecycle Operations
demonstrates the benefits of reducing procedural barriers while maintaining regulatory oversight.

Going forward, Punjab’s reform agenda should focus on strengthening financial sustainability,
modernising regulatory delivery mechanisms, and institutionalising independent regulatory oversight
through an autonomous State School Standards Authority. Such reforms would complement the state’s
existing strengths and help create a more balanced ecosystem that promotes accountability, innovation,
and educational growth.

By improving financial enablement and regulatory modernisation, Punjab is well positioned to evolve
from a strong-performing state into a national leader in school governance reform and ease of
operating schools.

because ultimately, the government and the private schools are
working for the benefit of the students. If the education becomes
child-centric and we look at the benefit of the students, I think
we can also improve the learning outcomes.

Policy Pathway
Sikkim’s regulatory framework provides some stability in compliance procedures and institutional
continuity, as reflected in its above-average performance on regulatory compliance and moderate
performance in school lifecycle operations. However, its overall score of 13.97 out of 100—the lowest
in the country—highlights deep structural weaknesses in the broader regulatory environment. Schools
face significant challenges in accessing regulatory information, navigating compliance requirements,
mobilising financial resources, and operating with confidence in enforcement processes. Given the
substantial role played by private schools in educating over two-fifths of students, future reforms should
focus on improving regulatory transparency, strengthening financial flexibility, and enhancing procedural
safeguards. Addressing these foundational constraints would significantly improve the ease of operating
schools while maintaining accountability and educational standards.

Policy Pathway
Tamil Nadu demonstrates that strong procedural safeguards can coexist with a relatively restrictive
regulatory framework. The state ranks among the top performers nationally in protection against arbitrary
regulatory action, providing schools with greater due-process protections, appeal mechanisms, and
predictability in enforcement. However, its overall score of 16.85 out of 100 highlights deeper structural
challenges within the regulatory environment. Schools continue to face significant difficulties arising
from weak regulatory accessibility, limited institutional autonomy, and procedural barriers affecting
institutional development. Given that private schools educate nearly half of all students in the state,
future reforms should focus on simplifying regulatory processes, improving transparency, and expanding
school-level decision-making authority. These reforms would allow schools to better leverage the stability
already present within Tamil Nadu’s regulatory framework while creating a more enabling environment
for innovation, sustainability, and educational choice.

“   That a private, un-aided, recognised school is not expected
to follow a system of accounting different from what is required
of a ‘not-for-profit institution’ under the Income-tax Act,
1961 and the ICAI Guidance Note dated 21.07.2005 [GN(A) 21],
which note specifically prescribes how schools are to maintain
their accounts. The DoE is not empowered to demand that a
school should maintain a different, parallel set of accounts
in accordance with the DoE’s diktat and to assess the funds
available with a school on that basis.
                                                               ”
                                          - Delhi Public School Vasant Kunj v. Government
                                                        of Delhi 2026 DHC 4590 para 144.4

Policy Pathway
Telangana has emerged as India’s leading regulatory environment for private schools, distinguished
by exceptional performance in regulatory compliance, institutional autonomy, and school lifecycle
operations. The state’s framework demonstrates that operational flexibility and regulatory accountability
can coexist within a high-performing education ecosystem.

The next generation of reforms should focus on strengthening safeguards against arbitrary regulatory
action and improving financial enablement while institutionalising regulatory excellence through an
independent State School Standards Authority. Such reforms would not only address the state’s remaining
weaknesses but also position Telangana as a national model for modern, transparent, and innovation-
oriented school governance.

By combining its existing strengths with stronger procedural protections and independent regulation,
Telangana can further consolidate its position as the benchmark state for enabling educational
entrepreneurship while safeguarding public accountability.

text:
Policy Pathway
Uttar Pradesh occupies a unique position within India’s school education landscape, serving the largest
school-going population in the country and educating more than half of its students through private
schools. The state’s regulatory framework demonstrates notable strength in financial mobilization,
providing schools with greater scope for financial sustainability and resource planning than is available
in most jurisdictions. However, these advantages are substantially diluted by high compliance burdens,
limited institutional autonomy, and challenges in navigating regulatory processes. As one of India’s largest
and most influential education ecosystems, even incremental improvements in regulatory efficiency could
have transformative effects on millions of students and thousands of schools. Future reforms should
focus on simplifying compliance requirements, improving regulatory accessibility, and empowering
schools with greater operational autonomy while preserving accountability safeguards. Such changes
would significantly enhance the ease of operating schools and strengthen the long-term sustainability of
educational provision across the state.

text:
Policy Pathway
Uttarakhand presents a regulatory environment with several foundational strengths but significant
structural gaps. The state performs above the national average in institutional autonomy and regulatory
compliance, suggesting that schools generally operate within a reasonably consistent compliance
framework and retain some operational flexibility. It also performs relatively well in school lifecycle
operations, reducing barriers to institutional continuity. However, these advantages are undermined by the
complete absence of enabling provisions for financial mobilization and comparatively weak protections
against discretionary regulatory action. Given that private schools educate nearly six out of every ten
students in the state, strengthening the long-term sustainability of the sector is critical for maintaining
educational access and choice. Future reforms should focus on enabling financial viability, improving
regulatory transparency, and strengthening procedural safeguards while preserving the state’s existing
strengths in compliance management and institutional flexibility. Such measures would create a more
balanced and enabling regulatory environment for schools across Uttarakhand.

text:
Annexure 1
Definitions of Indicators

DOMAIN 1 - Regulatory Clarity, Predictability & Accessibility (2 Indicators, 41 sub-indicators)
Indicator 1: Regulatory Transparency - This indicator assesses the accessibility of regulatory information
relevant to school. It examines the availability of laws, manuals, circulars, guidance documents, and digital
support systems through official State Education Department websites and portals.

Indicator 2: Procedural Predictability - This indicator evaluates if schools are able to anticipate
administrative decision-making with certainty. Accordingly, it maps clarity of timelines, approving
authorities, and codification of administrative procedures.

DOMAIN 2 - Regulatory Compliance ( 7 Indicators, 27 sub-indicators)
Indicator 1: Compliances during school establishment - This indicator covers procedural and financial
requirements for obtaining permission to establish schools. It includes certifications, fees, deposits and
other compliance-related conditions during the stage of opening schools.

Indicator 2: Infrastructure norms for school recognition - This indicator broadly covers all infrastructure
related requirements mandated by the laws for getting the schools recognized by the state governments.
It includes compliances like facilities provided, classroom sizes, and nature of land, etc.

Indicator 3: Procedure for Fee Hike - This indicator covers different steps and documentary requirements
imposed on schools for seeking approval for fee hikes.

Indicator 4: Staffing requirements - This indicator assesses the staffing requirements, particularly the prescribed
teacher-student ratios. It examines the extent to which staffing standards are fixed through the legal norms.

Indicator 5: Financial Reporting - This indicator evaluates accounting and financial disclosure-related
obligations imposed on schools. It also assesses the frequency of such reporting and the consequences for
non-compliance with these requirements.

Indicator 6: Affiliation related requirements - This indicator covers certifications relevant for obtaining
affiliation from state boards of education.

Indicator 7: Capital requirements for recognition- This indicator measures the financial prerequisites
imposed on schools as part of the recognition process. The sub-indicators assess capital adequacy and
deposit related requirements during this stage.

DOMAIN 3 - Operations without Arbitrary Regulatory Action (4 indicators, 52 sub-indicators)
Indicator 1: Inspections- This indicator evaluates school inspection procedures on the basis of their
safeguards and objectivity. In doing so, it highlights the scope of discretionary risk, along with the
availability of procedural protections and appellate mechanisms for schools.

Indicator 2: Withdrawal of Affiliation - This indicator analyses procedural protections available in cases
where the state boards withdraw their affiliation granted to schools.

Indicator 3: Withdrawal of approvals and takeover powers - This indicator evaluates the procedural
protections available during the withdrawal of approvals such as permission to establish and school
recognition, as well as during the takeover of school management or property. It also examines the
availability of appellate mechanisms for schools in such cases.

Indicator 4: Parent Grievance Redressal - This indicator evaluates the procedural safeguards available to

text:
schools in fee-related complaints raised by parents. It examines the availability of hearing opportunities,
penalties, and appellate mechanisms in such proceedings.

DOMAIN 4 - Financial Sustainability & Resource Mobilization (3 indicators, 18 sub-indicators)
Indicator 1: Fee Collection and Utilization of Funds - This indicator assesses regulatory controls over fee
structures. It also examines limitations on the use of school revenues and savings by schools.

Indicator 2: Mechanism for fee approvals - This indicator covers processes and approvals involved for fee
fixation and its revision. It determines the extent of regulatory oversight in fee-related decision-making
and procedural safeguards available in these approval processes.

Indicator 3: Regulations on capitation fee - This indicator assesses the extent to which the legal framework
restricts or permits the charging of capitation fees by schools. It examines prohibitions, exceptions, and
penalties relating to the charging of capitation fees under the applicable legal framework.

DOMAIN 5: School Lifecycle Operations ( 5 Indicators, 16 sub-indicators)
Indicator 1: School Establishment Requirements - This indicator covers steps involved for obtaining a
permission to establish schools and the scope of power available with authorities to withdraw such
permission.

Indicator 2: School Operation and Expansion Requirements - This indicator broadly covers permissions
required for school operations and upgradation, which includes approvals and state government
recognition.

Indicator 3: Board Affiliation - The indicator covers procedures for obtaining and retaining board affiliation.
This includes norms for inspections, and consequences arising from violation of affiliation norms.

Indicator 4: Voluntary Exit - This indicator assesses if permissions are required if the school wishes to
voluntarily close itself, and punishments for violating such norms.

Indicator 5: Forced Exit - This indicator assesses the conditions under which the government has powers to
close down a school or take over its property.

DOMAIN 6: Institutional Autonomy (2 Indicators, 10 sub-indicators)
Indicator 1: Payment of Staff Salaries - This indicator analyses the extent schools have power to fix staff
salaries.

Indicator 2: Self Governance - This indicator covers the regulatory requirements governing constitution,
composition, functioning, and reconstitution of School Management Committees (SMCs). It also examines
if the authorities have power to take actions against the SMC.

Authors’ Bio
Dr Animesh Kumar
Dr Animesh Kumar is a Senior Legal Researcher at CCS. As an advocate, he has argued various matters
related to civil and criminal disputes at various judicial forums across India. His doctoral research
investigated Women’s political participation in the PRIs in the State of Bihar. He has published various
articles on education. His specialisation includes constitutional law, with a research focus on women’s
political participation. At the Centre for Civil Society, he has authored the Nagaland State Regulatory
Profile which maps the laws governing K-12 education system in the State and reviewed multiple working
papers dealing with school education.

Animesh is the recipient of the Best Paper Presentation Award 2024 at ICRE 2.0 at Nirma University,
Gujarat (India). He has served as Co-Chair for numerous technical sessions at national and international
seminars and conferences. He has also edited three scholarly volumes titled Decentralization in India,
Alternative Dispute Resolution in India, and Law & Social Change. Additionally, Animesh is associated
with various international & national journals as an editor and advisory editorial board member. He is the
Editor-in-Chief of a peer-reviewed journal, Lex Revolution, ISSN 2394-997X (Print), 3107-282X (Online).

Shaivy Maheshwari
Shaivy Maheshwari is an Advocate enrolled with the Bar Council of Delhi. She has pursued her LLM in
International Trade and Business Laws from NALSAR, Hyderabad and BALLB(H) from Symbiosis Law
School, Noida. At the Centre for Civil Society, Shaivy has authored Bihar State Regulatory Profile, which
maps laws, institutions, and education governance in Bihar; and co-authored a working paper on “For-
profit Schooling in India Law, Limits, and Loopholes.” Having previously worked at CCS, Shaivy brings
experience in the areas of public governance, education, and livelihood. Alongside trade and competition
law, she brings legal expertise particularly in the domain of Constitutional Law and Administrative Law.
Prior to joining CCS, she has interned with various think tanks and research organizations such as NITI

Nitesh Anand
Nitesh Anand is Associate Director, Policy Research & Training at the Centre for Civil Society (CCS) and
Advisor to the Department of Policy, Ministry of Education, Youth and Sport, Cambodia. A Friedrich-
Naumann-Stiftung Scholar, India Fellow, and graduate of the Technical University of Munich, Nitesh
works on education, governance, and regulatory reform across Asia, leading research, policy engagement,
and capacity-building initiatives with governments, think tanks, academic institutions, and civil society
organizations.

Current work explores liberalising educational governance, institutional innovation, regulatory
modernization, legal design, and participatory governance. Guided by a commitment to individual freedom
and effective public institutions, this work seeks to create enabling environments that expand opportunity,
strengthen accountability, and foster human flourishing.
